scenes.headline: How to tell if a PDF needs OCR
scenes.sub: pdf-inspector: parsing and arithmetic, no machine learning.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Hawthorn! Before you pay for OCR, it helps to know which PDFs need it. Here's how pdf-inspector decides, with no model at all.

scenes.text: Read each page's operators and fonts, not its pixels. No model needed.
scenes.say: The idea: read each page's own content stream. Count what its operators draw, check that its fonts decode, and spot dense newspaper layouts. No model needed.

steps.say: Open the PDF with one Rust crate, and sample eight pages spread through it, so a scanned cover can't condemn a whole annual report.
Scan each page's content stream: which operators show text, which draw paths, and which fonts they call.
Each page comes out text-based, scanned or mixed. The whole file takes under two hundred milliseconds.
Text pages become Markdown directly; only the rest go to OCR. Firecrawl reckons fifty-four percent of PDFs don't need OCR at all.

items.say: One: lots of path drawing, almost no text operators, few distinct characters. The text is drawn as outlines, and needs OCR.
Two: a font with no Unicode map decodes to garbage. It tries two fallbacks before flagging the page as garbled.
Three: dense multi-column prose reads badly even when it decodes. Those thresholds were tuned on a Wall Street Journal PDF and SEC filings.

scenes.title: Score, non-ML engines
scenes.note: Firecrawl's own benchmark, one M4 Pro, OCR off
scenes.say: On Firecrawl's own benchmark, against engines without models or OCR, it edges the next one by two thousandths, and runs about one point six times faster.

scenes.text: Not every classification problem needs a model. A bounded question can be answered by parsing and arithmetic.

recap: Text to Markdown, the rest to OCR
scenes.say: To recap: sample the pages, read their operators, and send only the pages that need it to OCR.
